narrative.headline: Routine-sounding dependency refresh from a first-time author introduces a credential-harvesting postinstall hook, two look-alike packages and a repointed lodash tarball; 21 Critical findings in total
narrative.what_is_in_the_app: The application spans 31 components (25 packages, 13 direct and 12 transitive, max depth 2) across npm (7), PyPI (10), Maven (8), GitHub Actions (3), URL (2) and Docker (1), scoped mostly to prod (26) with 4 CI and 1 dev. The five tracked apps are the ci workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml), a Dockerfile, com.acme:notifier@1.0.0 (notifier/pom.xml), acme-orders@1.0.0 (package.json) and worker (worker/requirements.txt). The OSV.dev lookup flagged 16 vulnerable components across 141 advisories, including long-standing Maven and Python issues such as log4j-core@2.14.1 (F-007), jackson-databind@2.9.8 (F-008) and commons-text@1.9 (F-010).
narrative.what_changed: Commit 8cad42e from first-time author fastbuilds42, messaged 'chore: routine dependency refresh', touches six build and dependency files: the CI workflow, the Dockerfile, package.json and package-lock.json, worker/requirements.txt, and a newly added scripts/setup.js. It adds fastbuilds42/node:latest, fastbuilds42/cache-helper@main, crossenv@7.0.3, python3-dateutil@2.8.1, urllib3@2.8.0 and two URL-sourced shell scripts, and rewrites the lodash@4.17.15 lockfile entry while leaving its version string unchanged. 25 of the 41 findings are new in this change, and F-018 flags the commit itself as a suspicious first-time-contributor update to build controls.
narrative.what_appears_risky: The change concentrates risk in the install and build path rather than in application code. A new postinstall hook runs scripts/setup.js, which spawns shell commands, reads credential environment variables and decodes a base64-hidden endpoint (F-001); the triage agent assessed this as suspicious with high confidence. Two look-alike packages, crossenv@7.0.3 (F-004, F-012) and python3-dateutil@2.8.1 (F-006, F-013), are documented-malicious and typosquat matches, and the triage agent assessed both as likely malicious. lodash@4.17.15 keeps its version but gains a new integrity hash and resolves from npm-mirror.example.invalid (F-005, F-020, F-021) — the triage agent assessed the lockfile rewrite as likely malicious — while CI combines pull_request_target checkout of PR code, NPM_TOKEN piped to a downloaded script, write-all permissions and an unpinned third-party action (F-002, F-003, F-014, F-015, F-016). Separate from this change, the pre-existing vulnerable dependencies remain the largest block by count, led by F-007 and F-008.

top_concerns.why: A newly added postinstall script runs shell commands, reads token/credential environment variables and hides its endpoint in base64, giving it code execution on every install.
crossenv@7.0.3 was added as a direct dev dependency and is a documented malicious package, independently matched as a typosquat of 'cross-env' in F-012.
lodash@4.17.15 is unchanged in package.json but its lockfile integrity hash and source changed, corroborated by F-020 (non-registry host) and F-021 (rewritten resolved/integrity entry).
python3-dateutil@2.8.1 was added to the production worker requirements and is a documented malicious package, also flagged as a look-alike in F-013.
The CI workflow passes the NPM_TOKEN secret to a downloaded script, in a workflow that also checks out PR code under pull_request_target (F-002) and grants write-all permissions (F-016).

caveats: Several ai_triage entries (e.g. F-031, F-033, F-034, F-035, F-039, F-041) reference finding IDs that do not appear in the findings list of this packet, so those verdicts are reported as agent inference and not tied to enumerated findings.

The vulnerability counts (F-007 through F-011, F-022 through F-024) are pre-existing components with new_in_change=false; they are not introduced by commit 8cad42e and should be triaged separately from the supply-chain anomalies.
F-025 counts lodash@4.17.15 as vulnerable independently of the lockfile tampering in F-005/F-020/F-021; the same component is therefore both a known-vulnerability and a provenance issue.
One ai_triage entry was produced by rules only because the model returned invalid JSON, so at least one verdict carries no semantic analysis.

F-001.rationale: scripts/setup.js combines child_process import (F-001/E1), enumeration of high-value credential variables such as NPM_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (F-001/E2), a base64-hidden HTTP endpoint decoded to telemetry.example.invalid (F-001/E3, F-001/E5) and host/user fingerprinting (F-001/E4); the in-file comment claiming it is an 'INERT, never executed' demo fixture (F-001/T1) is not evidence of safety and is exactly the kind of text a dropper would carry. The commit that added the script is a first-time author's single commit labelled 'chore: routine dependency refresh' yet it also introduces typosquat-shaped and remote-script components (crossenv@7.0.3, python3-dateutil@2.8.1, get.example.invalid/*.sh, fastbuilds42/*) (F-001/T2), and install scripts are blocked by policy unless allow-listed. No excerpt shows secret values actually being transmitted, so the exfiltration path is not fully proven and the verdict stays below likely_malicious.
benign_explanations: A CI/bootstrap helper that checks which build-related tokens exist before configuring a pipeline
A telemetry stub used to demonstrate scanner detections in a repository fixture
F-001.recommended_next_step: Human reviewer should read the full scripts/setup.js (not just the excerpted lines), confirm whether package.json wires it as postinstall, and check the provenance of the same-commit additions (fastbuilds42 images/deps, get.example.invalid shell scripts, crossenv and python3-dateutil pins) before any build or install is run.

F-012.rationale: The name 'crossenv' is a one-character imitation of the popular 'cross-env' (F-012/E2) and was pinned as a new direct dev dependency in the latest change (F-012/E1, F-012/T3), added by a first-time author in a commit that also pulls in several unrelated artefacts. Registry metadata shows a security-holding package with no real repository, only a handful of versions and a single maintainer, and the pinned version is not even present in the registry (F-012/T1). Most importantly, the same component carries a related finding documenting it as a malicious package, plus an install script and an unexpected-dependency finding (F-012/T2), which matches the typosquat pattern where imitators of cross-env stole environment variables at install time. The change metadata offers no provenance that would explain this as an intentional fork or scoped variant.
benign_explanations: Accidental misspelling of 'cross-env' by a developer intending to add the legitimate package
A legitimate fork or scoped variant of cross-env with a different name
F-012.recommended_next_step: Confirm with the developer whether 'cross-env' was intended, quarantine builds that install this dependency, and treat the commit by first-time author 'fastbuilds42' as untrusted; review the install script and the other artefacts added in the same change (setup.js, container images, bootstrap/ci-agent scripts) before any remediation.

F-013.rationale: The dependency name 'python3-dateutil' is a separator-variant imitation of the popular 'python-dateutil' (F-013/E2) and is pinned directly into the production worker requirements (F-013/E1). It was introduced as a new prod dependency in commit 8cad42e by a first-time author under the message 'chore: routine dependency refresh' (F-013/T3), and the registry lookup finds no such public package at all (F-013/T1). Most decisively, a related finding on the exact same component documents it as a known malicious package (F-006, cited in F-013/T2), so the typosquat heuristic is not a false positive here. The same commit also adds other high-risk components, which reinforces the pattern rather than weakening it.
benign_explanations: An internal or privately hosted fork intentionally named 'python3-dateutil' that the public registry simply does not index (F-013/T1 only rules out a public listing, not a private index).
A developer typo while pinning the legitimate 'python-dateutil' library.
F-013.recommended_next_step: Human reviewer should confirm the advisory behind the documented-malicious finding on this component, verify whether any private index actually serves this name, and check CI/Docker/script changes from the same commit (8cad42e) for credential exposure before any removal decision.

F-018.rationale: A first-time author changed build and dependency controls in commit 8cad42e while describing it as a routine dependency refresh, which understates the change (F-018/E1, F-018/E2, F-018/T1). The same change introduces multiple dependency/CI-related components, including an untrusted image reference and remote bootstrap scripts (F-018/T1), matching the playbook confirmation pattern of a new contributor altering build files alongside other dependency/CI changes. Registry and repository file context are absent (F-018/T2, F-018/T3), so malicious behaviour is not directly demonstrated, but the innocent explanation is weaker than the risk indicators. The commit message's 'routine' wording is not evidence of safety; the assessment rests on the changed files and added components.
benign_explanations: A new team member made a legitimate dependency and CI refresh that awaits review.
An automated or semi-automated dependency update used an unfamiliar author identity.
F-018.recommended_next_step: A human reviewer should inspect the full diff of scripts/setup.js, .github/workflows/ci.yml, Dockerfile, package.json, package-lock.json, and worker/requirements.txt, and verify the author's identity, review approvals, and approval status of the newly referenced images, packages, and remote bootstrap scripts.

F-019.rationale: The Dockerfile pulls its base image from a personal-namespace repository, docker.io/fastbuilds42/node:latest (F-019/E1), and the registry lookup shows no such public package exists, i.e. never published, removed or private (F-019/T1). That namespace matches the commit author of the change, a first-time contributor whose single 'routine dependency refresh' commit rewrote the Dockerfile and added several components at once (F-019/T2). The same Dockerfile also pipes a remote script from get.example.invalid into a shell (F-019/T3), and the image is additionally tagged with the forbidden mutable 'latest' tag (related finding F-032). The indicators line up far better with an untrusted/implanted base image than with an innocent vendor-image exception, but the packet contains no direct proof of malicious content inside the image, so I stop at suspicious.
benign_explanations: The organisation could operate a private registry mirror under a personal-looking namespace, which would explain the failed public lookup (F-019/T1).
A developer might legitimately publish a hardened Node base image from their own Docker Hub account.
F-019.recommended_next_step: Have a human reviewer confirm whether 'fastbuilds42' is an approved internal publisher and, if the image exists privately, pull and inspect its layers/digest; also review the curl|sh bootstrap in the same commit (F-019/T3) and why a first-time author bundled it with a 'routine dependency refresh'.

F-020.rationale: The lockfile resolves lodash@4.17.15 to https://npm-mirror.example.invalid/... (F-020/E1), a host outside policy.registries and not a listed corporate mirror, and the '.invalid' TLD is a reserved, non-resolvable domain rather than an internal Artifactory/Nexus/Verdaccio proxy. The change is new in the latest commit (F-020/T1, F-020/T2), made by a first-time author under a 'routine dependency refresh' message that also touches the Dockerfile, CI workflow, adds scripts/setup.js and pulls in unrelated components from 'fastbuilds42/*' and 'get.example.invalid' sources. On the same component, F-005 records a changed integrity hash/source for the same version, F-021 records lockfile drift against an unchanged package.json range, and F-020/T3 confirms the genuine package is published on registry.npmjs.org with no install scripts. This combination matches lockfile injection rather than a routine mirror switch, but no malicious payload in the substituted tarball has been demonstrated, so the evidence does not justify likely_malicious.
benign_explanations: A corporate npm mirror or caching proxy could legitimately be used
A developer may have pasted a placeholder/typo URL into the lockfile
F-020.recommended_next_step: Confirm with the platform team whether npm-mirror.example.invalid is an approved proxy; if not, review commit 8cad42e in full (Dockerfile, ci.yml, scripts/setup.js, package.json), compare the fetched tarball's content and hash against the registry.npmjs.org artifact, and check whether the new 'fastbuilds42/*' images and get.example.invalid scripts were intended.

F-021.rationale: The lockfile entry for lodash@4.17.15 was rewritten to point at an unapproved host while package.json still pins the same version (F-021/E1, F-021/E2, F-021/T2); the sha512 integrity hash also changed, so the tarball served from npm-mirror.example.invalid is not the artifact previously recorded from registry.npmjs.org. The policy allowlist contains only registry.npmjs.org and registry.yarnpkg.com with no corporate mirrors, so this host has no sanctioned explanation, and related findings on the same component independently flag the untrusted source and the changed hash (F-005, F-020). The change comes from a first-time author with a single commit labelled 'chore: routine dependency refresh' that also adds CI workflow edits, a Dockerfile base image from the author's namespace, a new scripts/setup.js and typosquat-style packages such as crossenv@7.0.3 (F-021/E3, F-021/T1). That combination — cross-host repointing plus hash substitution hidden inside an unrelated multi-file commit by a new contributor — matches the lockfile-injection pattern rather than a routine dependency refresh; no 'demo/test' safety claim is present, and none would outweigh the behaviour.
benign_explanations: npm update / npm dedupe within the allowed semver range — rejected because the version did not move and both host and hash changed (F-021/E2)
lockfile format upgrade — rejected because only the resolved/integrity fields differ, not lockfileVersion (F-021/T2)
corporate/self-hosted mirror — rejected because the policy allowlist has no corporate mirrors and the host is npm-mirror.example.invalid (F-021/E2)
F-021.recommended_next_step: Block the commit from merging until a reviewer fetches both tarballs and diffs them, compares the head integrity hash against registry metadata for the official package, and inspects the newly added scripts/setup.js, CI workflow edits and the author's other commits.

F-031.rationale: The new `postinstall` hook (F-031/E1) runs `node scripts/setup.js` on every install, and F-031/T1 shows the referenced script file was added in the same commit (8cad42e) by a first-time author whose 'chore: routine dependency refresh' message hides edits to CI, the Dockerfile and dependency files. That commit also pulls in unpinned remote sources and typosquat-shaped names (crossenv, python3-dateutil) plus scripts hosted on an invalid domain, which is far beyond a routine dependency refresh. The package is not on the install-script allow-list, so policy already blocks this by default. The package.json description claiming it is a 'demo target - do not install' (F-031/T1) is text written by the author and cannot be treated as proof of safety; the actual behaviour of scripts/setup.js is what matters and was not captured.
benign_explanations: Application's own lifecycle script that only builds or copies local files (playbook false-positive class)
Repository is described in package.json as a demo/SSCG target rather than a published library
Setup script may only perform local project bootstrapping with no network or credential access
F-031.recommended_next_step: Obtain and review scripts/setup.js at commit 8cad42e and its diff: check for network fetches, child_process execution, environment/credential reads, and confirm with the repository owners whether fastbuilds42 should have commit rights.

F-033.rationale: The added dev dependency crossenv@7.0.3 is flagged in related findings on the same component as a documented malicious package (F-033/T3: F-004), as a typosquat of 'cross-env' (F-012), and as carrying an install script not on the policy allow-list (F-041). Registry metadata independently confirms the name is a 'security holding package' whose repository is npm/security-holder and which has no real published release for this version (F-033/T2: this_version_in_registry=false, this_version_published=null). The change itself is not an innocent tooling addition: it comes from a first-time author with a single commit, an unexplained 'routine dependency refresh' message that also adds docker images, remote shell scripts from get.example.invalid, and a new setup.js (F-033/E2, F-033/T1). The dev scope and commit message wording do not mitigate this; install-time behaviour is what matters here.
benign_explanations: Developer intended to add the legitimate 'cross-env' helper for cross-platform npm scripts and mistyped the name
A dev-only build utility was added as part of an otherwise routine maintenance commit
F-033.recommended_next_step: Confirm removal of crossenv from package.json/package-lock.json and review the other components added in commit 8cad42e (fastbuilds42 images, get.example.invalid scripts, scripts/setup.js) for related compromise before any further builds run.

F-034.rationale: The added dependency python3-dateutil==2.8.1 (F-034/E1) is a look-alike of the popular python-dateutil, and the registry lookup finds no such public package (F-034/T2), which removes any innocent source for it. Graph context links this same component to a documented-malicious determination and a typosquat determination (F-034/T3), and the introducing commit 8cad42e is by a first-time author whose 'routine dependency refresh' also adds crossenv, an unpinned third-party image, and remote bootstrap/CI scripts (F-034/E2, F-034/T1) — far beyond a routine bump. The commit message asserting a routine refresh is not evidence of safety; behaviour and provenance point the other way. Confidence is high because typosquat naming, absent registry provenance and a documented-malicious verdict all converge on the same pin.
benign_explanations: A private fork of python-dateutil pinned under an internal name — rejected because the registry lookup shows no package at all and the change bundles unrelated additions
Genuine dependency refresh that mistyped the package name — weak, since the name is a typosquat of a widely used library and the same commit adds several other risky components
F-034.recommended_next_step: Confirm the intent of commit 8cad42e with the author/owner, check for any install-time resolution or import of python3-dateutil in worker code, and treat the other components added in the same change (crossenv, unpinned images, remote shell scripts) as part of the same review.

F-035.rationale: urllib3 itself is a long-lived, widely used PyPI package with 109 releases and project URLs (F-035/T2), so the package name alone is not malicious. The problem is the surrounding change: a first-time author with a single commit labelled "routine dependency refresh" (F-035/E2, F-035/T1) simultaneously touched the CI workflow, Dockerfile and lockfiles and pulled in unrelated components such as a personal Docker Hub image, a remote bootstrap/ci-agent script from an external host, and crossenv, which the playbook cites as the classic typosquat example (F-035/T1). The new urllib3 line is also unpinned (F-035/E1, F-035/T4), which violates the policy requiring exact Python pins, and the commit message gives no reason a worker service needs it (F-035/T3). The "routine refresh" wording is not evidence of safety; judged by behaviour and provenance the change is not an innocent feature addition, though nothing shows urllib3@2.8.0 itself to be malicious.
benign_explanations: A well-known package added legitimately by a maintainer (only partly plausible: the package is genuine, but the commit is not a feature commit that clearly needs it and the author is a first-time contributor).
A routine dependency refresh by an automated or contract build engineer (weakened by the unrelated Docker image, remote scripts and crossenv additions in the same commit).
F-035.recommended_next_step: Have a human review commit 8cad42e as a whole, not just this line: confirm the provenance/identity of the first-time author, why the personal Docker image and the bootstrap/ci-agent scripts from the external host were added, and the crossenv addition; separately, require urllib3 to be pinned to an exact version per policy before merge.

F-039.rationale: Rules-only assessment (no LLM: invalid JSON from deepseek after retry: JSONDecodeError: Unterminated string starting at: line 1 column 1204 (char 1203)). Playbook default for R09_UNPINNED_DEPENDENCY is 'needs_human_review'. No additional signals in the gathered evidence.
F-039.recommended_next_step: no lockfile in that ecosystem, so every build may resolve a different version; production scope

F-041.rationale: F-041/T2 shows that the registry entry for this name is now a 'security holding package' (repository git+https://github.com/npm/security-holder.git, latest 0.0.2-security) and that the flagged version is not actually present in the registry, which is the signature of a package pulled for abuse rather than a normal release. F-041/E1 records an install script (hasInstallScript: true), which per policy is blocked unless allow-listed, and this name is not on the allow-list. F-041/T3 ties the same component to a documented-malicious verdict, a typosquat match against the popular 'cross-env', and a newly added dev dependency. The name is one edit away from a popular package, has no genuine upstream repository, and ships an install-time hook — the classic typosquat-with-install-script profile (AP-01). Dev scope does not mitigate this: install scripts execute on developer machines and CI runners alike.
benign_explanations: Name similarity to 'cross-env' could be coincidental, and dev-scoped dependencies are sometimes treated as low-impact.
An install script could in principle be a legitimate build step, but the registry shows a security-holder placeholder rather than a real package with a build toolchain.
F-041.recommended_next_step: Confirm removal of crossenv from package.json/package-lock.json and check commit 8cad42e (new author fastbuilds42) for whether the install script or the added scripts/setup.js ran in CI and which credentials were exposed.
